label: W1a·1
title: Systems, the project team, and the 4 SDLC phases with their deliverables
hook: After this lesson you can say why we need a formal process, name the 5 team roles, and list the 4 SDLC phases with the main deliverable of each one.

cards.h: Why do we need a formal process?
cards.body:
Imagine Inha builds a new course-registration system by just starting to code. On registration day it crashes, the deadline moves, and half the features are missing. This happens a lot in real life.

The professor's slide (W1a-S4) gives 3 reasons for a formal process:

  1. Failures occur (too) often.
  2. Creating systems is not intuitive.
  3. Projects are late, over budget, or delivered with fewer features than planned.

So: "The System Analyst is the key person." The analyst designs a system to add value and must understand the business processes. The job is rewarding but challenging, and it needs specific skills.

Course facts (W1a-S2): midterm + final + two quizzes; news in the Telegram channel; a recommendation letter only for B+ or higher.

The word comes from Greek systema: an organized relationship between parts that work for one goal.

Definition (W1a-S7): a system is "an orderly grouping of interdependent components linked together according to a plan to achieve a specific goal."

Example: a Tashkent café ordering app. Menu screen, cart, kitchen screen and payment are components. They need each other. The goal: serve the customer fast.

3 basic constraints of a system:

  1. It has structure and behavior designed for a predefined objective.
  2. Interconnectivity and interdependence between the components.
  3. The organization's objectives have higher priority than the objectives of its subsystems. (If the payment part wants 5 extra checks but the café wants fast service, the café goal wins.)

cards.h: Who is on the project team? (W1a-S3)
cards.body:
The slide shows a funny photo: one man digs a hole and many people watch. Each watcher has a label (Project manager, System Analyst, Business Analyst, Manager, Head of department, Project Champion, Product owner, SCRUM Master...). The table next to it gives 5 roles:

RoleWhat they do
Business analystKey business aspects; how the system gives business value; designs new business processes and policies
Systems analystHow technology can improve business processes; designs new processes; designs the information system; checks IS standards
Infrastructure analystInfrastructure standards; infrastructure changes needed (servers, network)
Change management analystChange management plan + user training plan
Project managerManages the team; develops and monitors the project plan; assigns resources; primary point of contact

Tip: business analyst = "why, for the business"; systems analyst = "how, with technology". The slide shows "hange management / nalyst": it is a typo for change management analyst.

SDLC (Systems Development Life Cycle) = "the process of understanding how an information system (IS) can support business needs by designing a system, building it, and delivering it to users" (W1a-S8).

It has 4 phases (W1a-S9). Each phase has steps, techniques and deliverables (the documents or things it produces). Each phase also answers one focus question:

  • Planning: Why build this system? How to structure the project?
  • Analysis: Who, what, where and when?
  • Design: How will this system work?
  • Implementation: delivery and support of the completed system

Note: the W1b deck (S4) adds a 5th phase, Post production (maintenance), "probably the longest phase". Use 4 phases unless the question asks about maintenance.
cards.diagram:
flowchart LR P["Planning
Why build it?"] --> A["Analysis
Who, what, where, when?"] A --> D["Design
How will it work?"] D --> I["Implementation
Deliver and support"]

cards.body:
Steps (W1a-S10):

  1. Project initiation: develop or receive a system request; do a feasibility analysis: technical, economic, organizational.
  2. Project management: develop the work plan; staff the project; monitor and control it.

Deliverables (S11 table): System request, Feasibility study, Project plan (work plan, staffing plan, standards list, risk assessment).

Techniques named: project identification; technical / economic / organizational feasibility; time estimation, task identification, work breakdown structure, PERT chart, Gantt chart, scope management; project staffing, project charter; CASE repository, standards, documentation, timeboxing, risk management.

Registration example: the Dean's office sends a request "registration crashes every semester". The team checks: can we build it, is it worth the money, will people use it? (W3 and W4 go deeper.)

Steps (W1a-S12):

  1. Develop an analysis strategy: model the current system, formulate the new system.
  2. Gather the requirements: develop a system concept; create a business model of business data and business processes.
  3. Develop a system proposal.

Deliverable (S13): the System proposal = requirements definition + use cases + process models + data model.

Techniques: BPA, BPI, BPR (business process automation / improvement / reengineering); interview, JAD session, questionnaire, document analysis, observation; use case analysis; data flow diagramming; entity relationship modeling, normalization.

The proposal goes to the steering committee for approval (W1b-S4).

Design (S14, S15)Implementation (S16, S17)
Steps1. design strategy
2. architecture and interfaces
3. databases and file specifications
4. program design: what programs to write and what each does		1. construct: build (write code) and test
2. install: train the users
3. support (maintenance)
Main deliverableSystem specificationInstalled system
Other deliverablesalternative matrix, architecture report, hardware and software specification, interface design, physical process model, program design, database and file specification, physical data modeltest plan, programs, documentation, migration plan (conversion plan, business contingency plan, training plan), support plan, problem report, change request, post-implementation audit report
Some techniquesarchitecture design, hardware and software selection, interface prototype, program structure chart, denormalization, performance tuningprogramming, software and performance testing, conversion strategy selection, training, system maintenance, post-implementation audit

example.problem: A Tashkent café wants an online ordering app. For each SDLC phase, say one thing the team does and the main deliverable.
example.solution:
PhaseWhat the team doesMain deliverable
PlanningOwner writes the request; team checks technical, economic and organizational feasibility; makes a work planSystem request + feasibility study; project plan
AnalysisInterviews waiters and customers; models how orders flow today and in the new appSystem proposal
DesignChooses the architecture, designs screens and the databaseSystem specification
ImplementationCodes and tests the app, trains staff, supports itInstalled system

check.q: Why do we need a formal process? (W1a-S4)
check.a: Failures occur too often; creating systems is not intuitive; projects are late, over budget or have fewer features than planned. So the system analyst is the key person.

check.q: Name the 3 basic constraints of a system.
check.a: 1) structure and behavior for a predefined objective; 2) interconnectivity and interdependence of components; 3) the organization's objectives have higher priority than the subsystems' objectives.

check.q: Which role develops the user training plan?
check.a: The change management analyst (change management plan + user training plan).

check.q: Business analyst vs systems analyst: one difference?
check.a: Business analyst focuses on business value and new processes and policies; systems analyst focuses on how technology improves processes and designs the information system.

check.q: In which phase is feasibility analysis done, and what are its 3 types?
check.a: Planning (project initiation): technical, economic, organizational feasibility.

check.q: What is the primary deliverable of the Analysis phase, and what does it contain?
check.a: The system proposal: requirements definition, use cases, process models, data model.

exam.question: List the phases of the SDLC. For each phase give its main steps and its primary deliverable.
exam.answer:
1. Planning: project initiation (system request, feasibility: technical, economic, organizational) and project management (work plan, staffing, monitor and control). Deliverable: system request with feasibility study, and project plan.
  2. Analysis: analysis strategy (current and new system), gather requirements, system proposal. Deliverable: system proposal.
  3. Design: design strategy, architecture and interfaces, databases and files, program design. Deliverable: system specification.
  4. Implementation: construct (build and test), install (train users), support. Deliverable: installed system.

(Optional: W1b-S4 adds a 5th phase, post production / maintenance, the longest one.)
exam.diagram:
flowchart LR
  P[Planning] --> D1(["System request + feasibility study, project plan"])
  D1 --> A[Analysis]
  A --> D2([System proposal])
  D2 --> DS[Design]
  DS --> D3([System specification])
  D3 --> I[Implementation]
  I --> D4([Installed system])

memorize: Formal process because: failures often, not intuitive, late / over budget / fewer features
System = orderly grouping of interdependent components, linked by a plan, for a specific goal
3 constraints: structure + behavior; interdependence; organization goals over subsystem goals
5 roles: business analyst, systems analyst, infrastructure analyst, change management analyst, project manager
SDLC: Planning → Analysis → Design → Implementation (+ Post production in W1b-S4)
Deliverables: system request + feasibility study + project plan → system proposal → system specification → installed system
Feasibility: technical, economic, organizational
note: Slide typo: W1a-S3 table shows 'hange management / nalyst' (= change management analyst).

label: W1b·1
title: The systems analyst: career paths, soft vs hard skills, and the AI-augmented analyst
hook: After this lesson you can solve the professor's soft-vs-hard-skills exercise and explain what an AI-augmented analyst does.

cards.body:
People usually start in one of 2 entry-level jobs, then move to analyst jobs, then to senior jobs. Solid arrows = more common path, dashed = less common path.

  • Business function specialist → requirements analyst, business analyst (common), systems analyst (less common).
  • Programmer/analyst → business analyst, systems analyst, infrastructure analyst (common), requirements analyst (less common).
  • Top of the ladder: change management analyst, project manager, software architect.

cards.body:
Skill = the ability to do something well.

Hard skillsSoft skills
Whatprofessional skillssocio-psychological, personal skills
Measure?can be measured, assessed, verifieddifficult to measure or confirm at an interview
Proofa specific action, certificate, portfolioshows over time
Professiontied to a professiondo not depend on the profession
Examplesdriving a car, touch-typing, programming in a languageplanning your time and focusing on what is important, analytical thinking, justifying decisions, teamwork, teaching others

Soft skills are aimed at yourself or other people. They can be innate or learned from experience.

Trap: "analytical thinking" sounds technical, but on the slide it is a soft skill.

cards.h: The professor's exercise (S7): soft or hard?
cards.body:
He gave 6 statements. The answers were printed in blue:

#StatementAnswer
1Not related to a specific professionSoft
2Take a long time and are difficult to develop; need a lot of analysis of your own and other people's behaviorSoft
3Relatively easy to obtain through trainingHard
4Mastery is revealed over timeSoft
5Are tied to a specific professionHard
6Can be confirmed here and now; you can get a certificate or diplomaHard

Trick: the statements come in opposite pairs: 1↔5 (profession?), 2↔3 (hard or easy to learn), 4↔6 (over time vs here and now). Soft = 1, 2, 4. Hard = 3, 5, 6.
cards.diagram:
flowchart TD
  Q{"Can you prove it now, with a test or certificate?"} -->|Yes| H[Hard skill]
  Q -->|No| Q2{"Is it tied to one profession?"}
  Q2 -->|Yes| H
  Q2 -->|"No, it grows slowly with experience"| S[Soft skill]

cards.body:
An AI-augmented analyst is a human analyst who uses AI tools as cognitive partners: not replaced by AI, but enhanced by it. AI does routine, pattern-based, data-heavy work. The human does judgment, creativity, ethics and talking to stakeholders.

Division of labor (S9): interview: human reads body language, AI transcribes and summarizes · prioritization: human makes the final judgment, AI suggests · feasibility: human interprets constraints, AI estimates cost and time · UML: AI drafts, human reviews · documentation: AI first draft, human polishes · risks: human for business/political, AI for technical · ethics: human judges, AI flags bias.

6 new skills (S8): prompt engineering · AI output validation (detect hallucinations, bias, errors) · data literacy · ethical AI awareness · AI-tool orchestration (chain tools: ChatGPT → Copilot → AI tester) · model evaluation (precision vs recall).

AI parts of a system behave differently from normal code, so the design must change:

Normal OO assumptionAI realityDesign fix
same input → same outputprobabilisticconfidence scores, retries
state is visiblehidden weightsmodel versioning, snapshots
errors are bugsstatistical errors (false positives/negatives)human-in-the-loop fallback
predictable speedinference time variesasync, caching, batching
exhaustive testingstatistical validation (precision, recall, F1)model evaluation pipelines

5 AI-aware patterns: Model Wrapper (ChatbotModel.predict()) · Human-in-the-Loop (ReviewQueue.escalate_to_human()) · Model Version Manager (ModelRegistry) · Feature Store · Drift Detector (DriftMonitor.check_drift()).

4 AI-enhanced methodologies (S45):

  • AI-Augmented Agile: AI helps sprint planning, story estimation, backlog priority (Jira AI predicts which stories will miss the sprint).
  • MLOps: DevOps for ML models; version data, models and code together (DVC, MLflow).
  • LLM-Driven Development: LLMs generate code, tests, docs (GitHub Copilot, Cursor, Windsurf).
  • Automated Methodology Selection: AI reads project parameters (team size, unclear requirements, risk) and recommends a methodology.

S47 "Key takeaways" lists the learning outcomes of the deck: compare methodologies, modern analyst skills, the AI-augmented role, AI-aware OO design.

example.problem:
Soft or hard? (new practice items in the S7 style)
a) Can write SQL queries
b) Explains a difficult idea calmly to an angry client
c) Has a Scrum Master certificate
d) Plans their time and focuses on what is important
e) Can draw UML diagrams in a CASE tool
f) Works well in a team
example.solution:
a) Hard (tied to IT, can be tested now)
b) Soft (people skill, grows with experience)
c) Hard (certificate = confirmed here and now)
d) Soft (listed as soft on S6)
e) Hard (professional, can be shown in a portfolio)
f) Soft (teamwork is on the S6 soft list)

check.q: Define a skill, a hard skill and a soft skill.
check.a: Skill = ability to do something well. Hard = professional, measurable, verifiable by action/certificate/portfolio. Soft = socio-psychological/personal, not tied to a profession, hard to measure at an interview.

check.q: "Mastery is revealed over time." Soft or hard?
check.a: Soft (its pair, "can be confirmed here and now", is hard).

check.q: Is analytical thinking a hard or a soft skill on the slides?
check.a: Soft (W1b-S6).

check.q: What is an AI-augmented analyst?
check.a: A human analyst who uses AI as a cognitive partner: enhanced, not replaced. AI does routine/data work; the human does judgment, creativity, ethics, stakeholder interaction.

check.q: Which AI-aware pattern sends low-confidence predictions to a person?
check.a: Human-in-the-Loop (class ReviewQueue with escalate_to_human()).

exam.question: Determine which statements are true for describing soft skills, and which are true for hard skills: 1) Not related to a specific profession. 2) Take a long time and are difficult to develop. 3) Relatively easy to obtain through training. 4) Mastery is revealed over time. 5) Are tied to a specific profession. 6) Can be confirmed here and now; you can get a certificate or diploma.
exam.answer:
Soft skills: 1, 2, 4. Hard skills: 3, 5, 6.
Reason: hard skills are professional and can be measured and confirmed now (certificate); soft skills are personal, not tied to a profession, and show only over time.

memorize: Hard: measurable, certificate, tied to profession, easy to train
Soft: personal, not profession-tied, slow to develop, revealed over time; analytical thinking is SOFT
AI-augmented analyst: enhanced, not replaced; human = judgment, ethics, stakeholders
6 AI skills: prompt engineering, output validation, data literacy, ethical AI, tool orchestration, model evaluation
5 patterns: Model Wrapper, Human-in-the-Loop, Model Version Manager, Feature Store, Drift Detector

label: W1b·2
title: Methodologies: what they are, the 3 classes, and plan-driven vs agile
hook: After this lesson you can define a methodology, sort any methodology into Structured / RAD / Agile, and compare plan-driven and agile processes.

cards.h: A methodology is the recipe for the SDLC
cards.body:
The SDLC says what phases exist. A methodology says how to go through them: "a formalized approach to implementing the SDLC (a list of steps and deliverables)" (S12).

Where do methodologies come from? In-house (the company's own), from consulting firms, from the software vendor, or required by government projects.

⭐ How we tell methodologies apart (S13, bold): "the sequencing of the SDLC phases and the amount of time and effort devoted to each".

In the early days programmers jumped from a fuzzy request straight into writing code, like a student doing homework the night before. That caused the failures from W1a.

S3 shows many different SDLC pictures (5, 6, 7 phases...): there is no single official version. S4 describes 5 phases: Planning, Analysis (the key phase, ends with the system proposal approved by the steering committee), Design, Implementation, Post production (maintenance, the longest).

Plan-drivenAgile
All activities are planned in advance; progress is measured against the plan (S16)Planning is incremental; easy to change when customer requirements change
Used for high-level planning (S5)Used for low-level planning
Example: WaterfallExamples: XP, Scrum

⭐ "In practice, most practical processes include elements of both." "There are no right or wrong software processes."

S57 Rolling wave planning: a big high-level arc for the whole project, middle arcs per stage, small weekly/monthly plans. "Planning is Throughout the Project - Not a Stage."

S15: process standardization (less variety of processes in a company) gives better communication, less training time, and cheaper automated support.

flowchart LR
  subgraph HL["High-level plan: plan-driven, whole project"]
    L1(("low-level plan 1")) --> L2(("low-level plan 2"))
    L2 --> L3(("low-level plan 3"))
    L3 --> L4(("low-level plan 4"))
  end

cards.h: The 3 classes of methodologies (S17, S18, S26)
cards.body:
• Structured design (dominant in the 1980s): a formal step-by-step approach, phase after phase. → Waterfall, Parallel.
  • RAD, Rapid Application Development (1990s): get some part of the system to users quickly, so they understand it and suggest changes. → Phased, Prototyping (Throwaway prototyping follows on the slides).
  • Agile: programming-centric, less documentation. → eXtreme Programming (XP), SCRUM.

RAD speed-up tools (S26): CASE tools · JAD sessions · fourth-generation / visual programming languages (e.g. Visual Basic) · code generators.

RAD fixes "both weaknesses" of structured design. From S23, S24 and S31 these are: (1) a long wait before users see anything, and (2) it is hard to react when requirements change.

Trap: Phased and Prototyping are RAD, not structured. Parallel is structured.
cards.diagram:
flowchart TD
  M[Methodologies] --> ST["Structured, 1980s"]
  M --> RD["RAD, 1990s"]
  M --> AG[Agile]
  ST --> W[Waterfall]
  ST --> PA[Parallel]
  RD --> PH[Phased]
  RD --> PR[Prototyping]
  RD -.->|"shown next"| TP[Throwaway prototyping]
  AG --> XP[eXtreme Programming]
  AG --> SC[SCRUM]

cards.h: Agile development and the Agile Manifesto (S40, S41)
cards.body:
Agile = programming-centric methodologies that streamline the SDLC. Much modeling and documentation is removed; face-to-face communication is preferred. Every iteration is a complete small project: planning, requirements analysis, design, coding, testing, documentation. Cycles are short: 1–4 weeks.

Agile Manifesto: 4 values (left side valued more):

  1. Individuals and interactions over processes and tools
  2. Working software over comprehensive documentation
  3. Customer collaboration over contract negotiation
  4. Responding to change over following a plan

Trap: "while there is value in the items on the right, we value the items on the left more". The right side is not worthless.

cards.h: The 12 agile principles (S42, S43), short version
cards.body:
1. Deliver software early and continuously; satisfy the customer.
  2. Welcome changing requirements, even late.
  3. Deliver working software frequently.
  4. Customers and developers work together.
  5. Trust motivated people; give them tools and environment.
  6. Face-to-face talk is the best way to gather requirements.
  7. Working software is the primary measure of progress.
  8. Sustainable pace: no burnout.
  9. Technical excellence and good design.
  10. Simplicity: avoid unnecessary work.
  11. Self-organizing teams make the best designs.
  12. Teams regularly reflect and improve.

Memory hook for a café app team: "Ship often, welcome change, talk face to face, measure by working app, keep it simple, rest, improve."

cards.h: XP and Scrum, the two agile examples (S54–S56)
cards.body:
Extreme Programming (XP): "perhaps the best-known and most widely used agile method".

  • New versions built several times per day.
  • Increments delivered to customers every 2 weeks.
  • All tests run for every build; a build is accepted only if the tests pass.
  • Principles (S55): small frequent releases; full-time customer with the team; pair programming, collective ownership, no long working hours; change through regular releases; simplicity through constant refactoring.

Scrum (S56): named after the rugby restart. Idea: however much you plan, chaos breaks out when coding starts, so you react and "sprint" with the ball. At the end of each sprint a system is delivered to the customer.

⚠️ W1b-S56 says a sprint lasts "thirty working days", but W2 says "one month or less" / "1–4 week sprint". Quote the deck the question comes from; for general Scrum questions use W2.

cards.h: 6 project characteristics that decide the methodology (S14)
cards.body:
Before choosing, ask 6 questions about the project:

  1. Clarity of user requirements: do users and analysts understand what is needed?
  2. Familiarity with technology: has the team used this technology before?
  3. System complexity: many features, many integrations, many departments?
  4. System reliability: must it never go down?
  5. Short time schedules: is the deadline tight?
  6. Schedule visibility: do sponsors want to see progress often?

These 6 are exactly the rows of the "Which Methodology to Use?" table (S46). You will use that table at the end of the drawing lessons.

example.problem: Plan-driven or agile? 1) "All process activities are planned in advance." 2) "Planning is incremental." 3) "Used for high-level planning." 4) "Customer collaboration over contract negotiation." 5) "Mostly used for large systems engineering projects developed at several sites." 6) "Changing requirements are embraced regardless of when they occur."
example.solution: 1) Plan-driven (S16) · 2) Agile (S16) · 3) Plan-driven (S5) · 4) Agile (Manifesto, S41) · 5) Plan-driven: this is Waterfall (S23) · 6) Agile (S42)

check.q: What is a methodology?
check.a: A formalized approach to implementing the SDLC: a list of steps and deliverables.

check.q: What is the important factor for categorizing methodologies?
check.a: The sequencing of the SDLC phases and the amount of time and effort devoted to each (S13).

check.q: Name the 3 classes of methodologies and the examples of each from S17.
check.a: Structured: Waterfall, Parallel. RAD: Phased, Prototyping. Agile: XP, Scrum.

check.q: Name the 4 RAD speed-up tools.
check.a: CASE tools, JAD sessions, fourth-generation / visual programming languages (Visual Basic), code generators.

check.q: XP: how often are builds made and increments delivered?
check.a: Builds several times per day; increments every 2 weeks; all tests run on every build.

check.q: Which approach is used for high-level planning and which for low-level planning?
check.a: Plan-driven for high-level, agile for low-level (S5).

exam.question: Classify these methodologies into the three classes and describe each class in one sentence: Waterfall, Phased, XP, Parallel, Prototyping, Scrum.
exam.answer:
Structured design (Waterfall, Parallel): formal step-by-step approach, moving logically from one phase to the next (dominant in the 1980s).
RAD (Phased, Prototyping): adjusts the SDLC phases to get some part of the system to users quickly so they can suggest revisions; uses CASE, JAD, visual languages, code generators (1990s).
Agile (XP, Scrum): programming-centric; short 1–4 week iterations, each a complete mini-project; less documentation, face-to-face communication.
exam.diagram:
flowchart TD
  M[Methodologies] --> ST[Structured]
  M --> RD[RAD]
  M --> AG[Agile]
  ST --> W[Waterfall]
  ST --> PA[Parallel]
  RD --> PH[Phased]
  RD --> PR[Prototyping]
  AG --> XP[XP]
  AG --> SC[Scrum]

memorize: Methodology = formalized approach to implementing the SDLC (steps + deliverables)
Categorized by: sequencing of SDLC phases + time and effort on each
Structured (1980s): Waterfall, Parallel · RAD (1990s): Phased, Prototyping · Agile: XP, Scrum
RAD tools: CASE, JAD, 4GL/visual languages, code generators
Plan-driven = planned in advance, high-level · Agile = incremental, low-level · no right or wrong process
Manifesto: individuals, working software, customer collaboration, responding to change
XP: builds several times/day, increments every 2 weeks, all tests every build
6 characteristics: clarity of requirements, familiarity with technology, complexity, reliability, short schedule, schedule visibility
note: Slide conflict: W1b-S56 says a Scrum sprint is 'thirty working days'; W2 says 'one month or less' (1–4 weeks).

label: W1b·3
title: Draw it like the professor: Waterfall, V-model and Parallel
hook: After this lesson you can draw the Waterfall, V-model and Parallel diagrams from memory, exactly in the slide style, and write 2–3 lines plus a pro and a con under each (Quiz 1 asked Waterfall and Parallel).

cards.h: The drawing language of the slides
cards.body:
All methodology pictures in W1b use the same symbols. Learn them once, then every diagram is easy:

  • Rectangle = one phase (Planning, Analysis, Design, Implementation).
  • Solid curved arrow = go forward to the next phase.
  • Dashed wavy arrow back to the previous phase = you can go back and fix things.
  • Rounded box = an output: "System", "System version 1", "System prototype", "Design prototype".
  • Dotted ellipse around boxes = a group that runs on its own or repeats (a subproject, one version).
  • Stacked block (phases drawn touching, one on top of another) = these phases happen at the same time.

Recipe for any "Depict graphically" question: 1) write the title; 2) draw the boxes in the right shape; 3) add solid forward arrows; 4) add dashed back arrows; 5) end in a rounded output box; 6) under it, write 2–3 lines on how it works + 1 pro + 1 con.
cards.diagram:
flowchart LR A[Phase box] -->|"solid: go forward"| B[Next phase] B -.->|"dashed wavy: go back"| A B --> O(["Rounded box: output, e.g. System"]) K["Stacked block:
Analysis
Design
Implementation
all at the same time"]

cards.body:
Shape: a staircase going down to the right, like water falling from step to step.

Draw: Planning (top left) → Analysis → Design → Implementation → rounded System (bottom right). 4 solid forward arrows. 3 dashed wavy back arrows: Analysis→Planning, Design→Analysis, Implementation→Design. No arrow back from System.

How it works: a "cascade from one phase to another". It is plan-driven: "you must plan and schedule all of the process activities before starting work on them" (S21).

Pro: the plan-driven nature helps coordinate work; used for large systems engineering projects developed at several sites (S23).

Con: "inflexible partitioning of the project into distinct stages makes it difficult to respond to changing customer requirements"; "few business systems have stable requirements"; the system arrives only after completion.

When to use: requirements are well understood and changes will be limited. S46: Good for complex and reliable systems, Poor for the other 4 rows.
cards.diagram:
flowchart TD
  P[Planning] --> A[Analysis]
  A --> D[Design]
  D --> I[Implementation]
  I --> S([System])
  A -.-> P
  D -.-> A
  I -.-> D

cards.body:
Shape: a big letter V. Down the left = define and design. Bottom point = coding. Up the right = testing. In the middle, teal rounded boxes = test designs, with dashed arrows from the left side to them and from them to the matching test on the right.

Draw: left slope: Analysis → Design → Implementation (coding) at the bottom. Right slope: Unit testing → Integration testing → System testing → Acceptance testing (top right). Middle: Analysis ⇢ Acceptance test design ⇢ Acceptance testing; Design ⇢ System, Integration, Unit test design ⇢ the matching tests. Add a big down arrow on the left and a big up arrow on the right.

Key fact: acceptance tests are planned in Analysis; system, integration and unit tests are planned in Design.

Pros, cons, when to use (not on the slides, general knowledge): + every test is planned early, so testing is strong; − as rigid as waterfall; use it when quality and reliability matter and requirements are stable. Not rated in S46.
cards.diagram:
flowchart TD
  AN[Analysis] --> DE[Design]
  DE --> IM["Implementation (coding)"]
  IM --> UT[Unit testing]
  UT --> IT[Integration testing]
  IT --> ST[System testing]

cards.h: ③ Parallel development (S24, S25) — Structured, Quiz 1 V3
cards.body:
Shape: starts like a waterfall (Planning → Analysis → one general Design), then splits into 3 subprojects, then joins again in Integration.

Draw:

  1. Planning → Analysis → Design, staircase, with dashed back arrows.
  2. From the general Design, 3 arrows to 3 dotted ellipses labelled Subproject 1, 2, 3. Inside each: Design → Implementation, with a dashed back arrow. Also a dashed back arrow from each subproject's Design to the general Design.
  3. All 3 Implementations → Integration → rounded System.

How it works: a general design for the whole system, then the project is divided into distinct subprojects that are designed and implemented in parallel; at the end the pieces are integrated and delivered.

Pro: reduces the time to deliver, so there is less chance that business changes cause rework.

Con: still one big delivery after completion (S31); the pieces must fit together at integration.

When to use: a big system that splits into independent parts and a short schedule. S46: like Waterfall, but Good for short time schedule.

flowchart TD
  P[Planning] --> A[Analysis]
  A --> D[General design]
  A -.-> P
  D -.-> A
  subgraph SP1["Subproject 1"]
    D1[Design] --> I1[Implementation]
    I1 -.-> D1
  end
  subgraph SP2["Subproject 2"]
    D2[Design] --> I2[Implementation]
    I2 -.-> D2
  end
  subgraph SP3["Subproject 3"]
    D3[Design] --> I3[Implementation]
    I3 -.-> D3
  end
  D --> D1
  D --> D2
  D --> D3
  I1 --> INT[Integration]
  I2 --> INT
  I3 --> INT
  INT --> SYS([System])

cards.h: Waterfall vs Parallel: do not mix them up
cards.body:
WaterfallParallel
ClassStructuredStructured
Shapeone staircasestaircase that splits into 3 ellipses and joins
Designoncegeneral design + a design inside each subproject
Extra boxnoneIntegration
OutputSystemSystem
Main problem it solves / hashas: inflexible to changing requirementssolves: long delay between analysis and delivery
S46 short schedulePoorGood

Common mistakes: forgetting the dashed back arrows; forgetting the rounded System box; in Parallel, forgetting the general Design before the split, the subproject labels, or the Integration box.

example.problem: S19 shows another waterfall: the first published model (Royce, 1970). Draw it and say how it differs from the S20 waterfall.
example.solution:
Staircase of 5 rounded boxes: Requirements definition → System and software design → Implementation and unit testing → Integration and system testing → Operation and maintenance. A feedback line runs along the bottom from Operation and maintenance, with an up-arrow into each of the 4 earlier boxes.
Difference: Royce names 5 engineering stages and feeds back from the end to every stage; the S20 class version uses the 4 SDLC phases, ends in a rounded System box, and goes back only one step at a time (dashed wavy arrows).
example.diagram:
flowchart TD
  R1[Requirements definition] --> R2[System and software design]
  R2 --> R3[Implementation and unit testing]
  R3 --> R4[Integration and system testing]
  R4 --> R5[Operation and maintenance]
  R5 -->|feedback| R1
  R5 -->|feedback| R2
  R5 -->|feedback| R3
  R5 -->|feedback| R4

check.q: In the Waterfall picture, how many dashed back arrows are there and where?
check.a: 3: Analysis→Planning, Design→Analysis, Implementation→Design. Nothing goes back from System.

check.q: Why is Waterfall called plan-driven?
check.a: You must plan and schedule all process activities before starting work on them (S21).

check.q: When is Waterfall appropriate, and where is it mostly used?
check.a: When requirements are well understood and changes are limited; mostly in large systems engineering projects developed at several sites.

check.q: In the V-model, in which phase are acceptance tests designed? And unit tests?
check.a: Acceptance test design comes from Analysis; system, integration and unit test designs come from Design.

check.q: What problem does Parallel development address, and what is its advantage?
check.a: Long delays between analysis and delivery. It reduces the time to deliver, so fewer business changes cause rework.

check.q: Which box exists in Parallel but not in Waterfall?
check.a: Integration (plus the subproject ellipses).

exam.question: ⭐ (Quiz 1, V3) Depict graphically: Parallel development methodology.
exam.answer:
Title: Parallel development-based methodology. Drawing: see the diagram: Planning → Analysis → general Design (with dashed back arrows), then 3 dotted ellipses Subproject 1, 2, 3, each Design → Implementation with a dashed back arrow, all joining in Integration → System.
Explanation: a general design is made for the whole system, then the project is divided into distinct subprojects that are designed and implemented in parallel; when all are complete they are integrated and the system is delivered.
Pro: reduces the time to deliver the system, so less chance that business changes cause rework.
Con: the system is still delivered only after completion, like waterfall.

memorize: Symbols: box = phase; solid arrow = forward; dashed wavy = back; rounded box = output; dotted ellipse = group; stacked block = same time
Waterfall: staircase P→A→D→I→(System), 3 dashed back arrows; plan-driven; inflexible; stable requirements
V-model: down = Analysis, Design; bottom = coding; up = unit → integration → system → acceptance testing
Acceptance test design ← Analysis; system/integration/unit test design ← Design
Parallel: P→A→general D → 3 subprojects (D→I) → Integration → (System); faster delivery
Royce 1970: 5 stages, feedback from Operation and maintenance to all
note: The slides do not label the dashed wavy arrows; reading them as 'go back to the previous phase' is the standard interpretation. V-model pros/cons are not on the slides.

label: W1b·4
title: Draw it like the professor: Phased, Prototyping, Throwaway prototyping, Agile — and choose the right one
hook: After this lesson you can draw the Phased (asked twice in Quiz 1), Prototyping, Throwaway and Agile diagrams from memory, and pick a methodology with the S46 table.

cards.h: ④ Phased (iterative) development (S27, S28) — RAD, Quiz 1 V1 and V4
cards.body:
Idea: the system is split into versions built one after another. Version 1 has the most important features. Users start using it, and their experience feeds version 2.

Draw:

  1. Planning → Analysis (overall concept), with a wavy back arrow. These appear once.
  2. Then 3 dotted ellipses, going down-left like stairs. Each has Analysis → Design → Implementation with dashed back arrows.
  3. Each ellipse ends in a rounded System version 1 / 2 / 3.
  4. A long arrow from System version 1 back up into the Analysis of ellipse 2, and from version 2 into the Analysis of ellipse 3.

Pros (S31): quickly gets a useful system into users' hands; business value sooner; users find important new requirements sooner.

Con (S32): users work with a system that is intentionally incomplete. Fix: put the most important features in version 1 and manage expectations.

When to use: you need value early and can split the system into versions. S46: never Poor; Excellent for short schedule and schedule visibility.
cards.diagram:
flowchart TD
  P[Planning] --> A0[Analysis]
  A0 -.-> P
  subgraph V1["Version 1"]
    A1[Analysis] --> D1[Design]
    D1 --> I1[Implementation]
    D1 -.-> A1
    I1 -.-> D1
  end
  subgraph V2["Version 2"]
    A2[Analysis] --> D2[Design]
    D2 --> I2[Implementation]
    D2 -.-> A2
    I2 -.-> D2
  end
  subgraph V3["Version 3"]
    A3[Analysis] --> D3[Design]
    D3 --> I3[Implementation]
    D3 -.-> A3
    I3 -.-> D3
  end
  A0 --> A1
  I1 --> S1([System version 1])
  S1 --> A2
  I2 --> S2([System version 2])
  S2 --> A3
  I3 --> S3([System version 3])

cards.h: Iterative vs incremental (S29, S30): the Mona Lisa
cards.body:
S29: the 3 most popular approaches to the iterative model are incremental, iterative, iterative-incremental. S30 explains them with the Mona Lisa:

  • Iterative: draw the whole picture as a rough sketch, then a coloured draft, then the finished painting. Each round improves everything.
  • Incremental: paint one finished piece (the face), then add the body, then the background. Each round adds a complete part.
  • Iterative-incremental: both: add parts and improve them each round. (Phased and agile work like this.)

Café app example: iterative = a simple version of the whole app, then a better one; incremental = first only the menu, then add payment, then add delivery.

Idea: Analysis, Design and Implementation happen at the same time and repeat in a cycle. You quickly build a system prototype, "a quick-and-dirty program that provides a minimal amount of features", show it, and improve it until the system is complete.

Draw: Planning (box) → a stacked block [Analysis / Design / Implementation], dashed wavy arrow back to Planning. Block → rounded System prototype. A line from the prototype back into the block (the repeat loop). Prototype → Implementation → rounded System.

Prototype uses (S35): requirements elicitation and validation; exploring design options and UI; back-to-back tests.

Pros (S36): better usability; closer match to users' real needs; better design quality; better maintainability; less development effort.

Cons (S37): leaves out functionality; error checking and recovery may be missing; focuses on functional, not non-functional requirements (reliability, security).

When to use: unclear requirements, tight deadline, sponsors want to see progress. S46: Excellent on these 3; Poor for unfamiliar technology, complex and reliable systems.
cards.diagram:
flowchart LR P[Planning] --> B["Analysis
Design
Implementation"] B -.-> P B --> SP([System prototype]) SP -->|"repeat"| B SP --> I[Implementation] I --> S([System])

cards.body:
Idea: build a design prototype only to learn (try a risky or unclear part), then throw it away and build the real system properly.

Draw: Planning → Analysis (staircase, dashed back arrows) → stacked block [Analysis / Design / Implementation] (dashed arrow back to Analysis). Block → rounded Design prototype, with a line back into the block (loop). From the block's top, a second arrow to the real build: Design → Implementation (dashed back arrow) → rounded System.

Difference from ⑤: output is a Design prototype, not a System prototype, and it does not become the system.

Why throw it away (S38, in red) — "not a good basis for a production system": 1) may be impossible to tune for non-functional requirements; 2) normally undocumented; 3) structure degraded by rapid change; 4) probably won't meet organizational quality standards.

When to use: unclear requirements and new technology and a complex or reliable system. S46: the only one Excellent for unfamiliar technology; Excellent on 4 rows; never Poor; but only Good for short schedule.
cards.diagram:
flowchart LR P[Planning] --> A[Analysis] A -.-> P A --> B["Analysis
Design
Implementation"] B -.-> A B --> DP([Design prototype]) DP -->|"repeat"| B B -->|"real build"| D[Design] D --> I[Implementation] I -.-> D I --> S([System])

cards.body:
Idea: all 4 phases are done together in one short cycle (1–4 weeks). Every cycle ends with a working system, and then the next cycle starts again from Planning.

Draw: one stacked block with all 4 phases [Planning / Analysis / Design / Implementation]. A line from the bottom of the block to a rounded System, and a line from System back to the top of the block (Planning). That's it: the simplest picture.

Pros (from S40–S43): working software early and often; welcomes changing requirements; little documentation overhead; face-to-face communication; adapts to the current business environment.

Cons (general knowledge, not on the slides): little documentation; needs an always-available customer and a skilled, disciplined team; hard for very large or complex systems.

When to use: unclear or changing requirements and a short schedule. S46 rates XP: Excellent for unclear requirements and short schedule; Good for reliable systems and visibility; Poor for unfamiliar technology and complex systems.

3-step method: 1) mark the rows the story mentions; 2) cross out every methodology with a Poor on a marked row; 3) choose the one with the most Excellents.

Patterns: Phased and Throwaway are never Poor. Prototyping is Poor exactly where Throwaway is strongest. Waterfall has no Excellent at all. V-model and Scrum are not in the table.

example.problem: A Tashkent café wants an ordering app in 3 months. The owner cannot explain clearly what she wants, and she wants to see progress every week. The app is simple and the team knows the technology well. Which methodology does the S46 table suggest? What changes if the app had to be highly reliable?
example.solution:
Marked rows: unclear requirements, short time schedule, schedule visibility.
Cross out Poor: Waterfall (Poor on all 3), Parallel (Poor on unclear and visibility).
Count Excellents: Prototyping E, E, E = 3; Phased G, E, E = 2; XP E, E, G = 2; Throwaway E, G, G = 1.
→ Prototyping.
If reliability were also needed: Prototyping is Poor for reliable systems, so cross it out. Then Phased (G, E, E, G) and XP (E, E, G, G) tie with 2 Excellents each; Phased has no Poor anywhere and Excellent visibility, which the owner asked for, so Phased is a safe answer (explain your reasoning).

check.q: In the Phased diagram, where does the arrow from 'System version 1' go?
check.a: Into the Analysis box of the next ellipse (version 2): users' experience with version 1 feeds the analysis for version 2.

check.q: What is the major drawback of phased development, and how do you reduce it?
check.a: Users work with intentionally incomplete systems. Put the most important features in version 1 and manage users' expectations.

check.q: Prototyping vs Throwaway prototyping: two differences in the drawing.
check.a: Prototyping outputs a System prototype that grows into the system; Throwaway outputs a Design prototype that is discarded, and the real system is built on a separate Design → Implementation → System path. Throwaway also has a separate Analysis box before the stacked block.

check.q: Give the 4 reasons why throwaway prototypes should be discarded.
check.a: Impossible to tune for non-functional requirements; undocumented; structure degraded by rapid change; won't meet organizational quality standards.

check.q: Which methodology is the only one rated Excellent for unfamiliar technology?
check.a: Throwaway prototyping.

check.q: Iterative vs incremental in one sentence each.
check.a: Iterative: improve the whole thing each round (sketch → draft → final). Incremental: add one finished piece each round.

exam.question: ⭐ (Quiz 1, V1 and V4) Depict graphically: Phased development methodology.
exam.answer:
Title: Phased (iterative) development-based methodology. Drawing: Planning → Analysis once, then 3 dotted ellipses, each Analysis → Design → Implementation with dashed back arrows, each ending in a rounded System version 1, 2, 3; an arrow from each version into the Analysis of the next ellipse.
Explanation: the overall system is broken into a series of versions developed sequentially. The most important and fundamental requirements go into version 1. After version 1 is implemented, work begins on version 2, using the remaining requirements plus new ideas from users' experience with version 1. This continues until the system is complete or no longer in use.
Pro: a useful system reaches users quickly and gives business value sooner; users identify new requirements sooner.
Con: users work with an intentionally incomplete system, so expectations must be managed.

  A0 -.-> P

    A1[Analysis] --> D1[Design]
    D1 --> I1[Implementation]
  end
  subgraph V2["Version 2"]
    A2[Analysis] --> D2[Design]
    D2 --> I2[Implementation]
  end
  subgraph V3["Version 3"]
    A3[Analysis] --> D3[Design]
    D3 --> I3[Implementation]

memorize: Phased: P→A once, then ellipses (A→D→I) → System version n → arrow into next Analysis
Phased + : useful system fast, value sooner · − : intentionally incomplete
Prototyping: P → stacked block (A/D/I) ⇄ System prototype → Implementation → System
Prototyping benefits: usability, real needs, design quality, maintainability, less effort
Throwaway: P→A → stacked block ⇄ Design prototype (discarded); real build D→I→System
Discard because: can't tune non-functional, undocumented, degraded structure, below quality standards
Agile: one stacked block (P/A/D/I) → System → back to the block; cycles 1–4 weeks
S46: only Throwaway Excellent for unfamiliar technology; Phased and Throwaway never Poor; Waterfall no Excellent
note: Throwaway prototyping is not listed under RAD on S17, but it is taught right after Prototyping. Agile cons and V-model pros/cons are general knowledge, not slide content.
